title: The body: postures
hookLine: walking, he knows he walks; standing, sitting, lying down (MN 10)

lines: HOW ARE YOU SITTING RIGHT NOW?
cards: Quick question, and don't move: how are you sitting right now? Legs crossed? One foot tucked under?

Leaning on an elbow? A lot of people have to look down to find out. The whole day is spent in some position, standing in line, slumped on the couch, lying in bed scrolling, and hardly anyone is there for it.
The body is in one place, and the mind is somewhere else entirely. The next exercise in the Satipatthana Sutta sounds almost too simple to count.

teach.b: After the breath, the sutta turns to the four postures, in Pali the iriyapatha, the ways of moving. Walking, the practitioner knows, I am walking. Standing, I am standing.
Sitting, I am sitting. Lying down, I am lying down. However the body is placed, they know it that way.
That's the whole instruction. Then the chorus comes back: inside, outside, arising, passing, not clinging. It's tempting to laugh.
Of course I know I'm sitting.
But knowing it as a fact and knowing it as an experience are different. One is a thought about the body. The other is being in it: the weight on the seat, the feet on the floor, the slight lean.
And the four postures cover your entire life. You are always in one of them. The breath gave you a doorway you can use anytime.
The postures give you a second one, bigger and even harder to miss. No cushion or quiet room needed. The checkout line is standing.
The drive home is sitting. Falling asleep is lying down. One more gift.
Walking meditation, used in many monasteries, draws on lines like this one: monks and nuns walk slowly up and down a path, knowing each step.
For some people, walking is easier than sitting still, and the sutta names walking right alongside sitting.

how: Buddhist monastics and lay meditators often alternate sitting with walking meditation, pacing a short path slowly and knowing each step, and teachers encourage knowing the posture throughout the day.

o: a set of yoga poses that stretch and strengthen
feeling each posture: walking, standing, sitting, lying
keeping a straight back so you can meditate well

games.q: match each posture to where it shows up.

s: the sutta treats walking as a real meditation posture
walking, standing, sitting and lying down are all named.
knowing you're sitting is the same as thinking 'I'm sitting'
the practice is feeling the posture, not just knowing it as a fact.
you must fix your posture before you can know it
the sutta says: however the body is placed, know it that way.

games.q: you're slumped on the couch and remember today's practice. what does the sutta ask?
o: sit up straight first; slumping doesn't count.
know it: however the body is placed, know it that way.
wait until you're on a cushion.
games.why: the instruction is to know the posture as it is. the couch counts.

practice: Stay exactly how you are, without fixing your posture first, and just know it: I am sitting, or standing, or lying down. Feel where the body touches the seat, the floor or the bed, and the shape you're making.
Then straighten a little, slowly, knowing that too, and settle back into the plain knowing of the posture.

wordCard.voice: The body, postures. Walking, standing, sitting, lying down: in whatever way the body is placed, know it that way.

orig.note: Pali iriyāpatha: the postures, literally the ways of moving.

carryVoice: Your line: I know I'm sitting. Wherever you are, the posture is already there to know. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the four postures

sources.work: Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses (Buddhaghosa)
